chats.title: LST vs air temperature for heat maps

messages.text: I'm building a heat-vulnerability map for a mid-sized city and the standard approach seems to be pulling land-surface temperature from a thermal satellite band and overlaying it with census vulnerability indicators. But I keep reading that surface temperature isn't what people actually experience. Is the difference between land-surface temperature and air temperature big enough that it would change which neighbourhoods get flagged as hotspots?

It can be, yes. Land-surface temperature measures the skin temperature of whatever the sensor sees: rooftops, asphalt, tree crowns. On a sunny afternoon a dark roof can be 30 degrees hotter than the air two metres above the street. Air temperature at pedestrian height is smoothed by mixing and advection, so its spatial pattern is much flatter. The ranking of neighbourhoods often stays broadly similar, but the magnitude of differences shrinks, and some places flip, for example areas with lots of flat industrial roofs look extreme in LST but may be only modestly warmer at street level. Overpass timing also matters, since most thermal satellites pass in the morning, not at peak afternoon heat.

That's exactly my worry. The industrial zone on the east side lights up like a furnace in my LST layer, but almost nobody lives there, while some dense residential blocks with lots of shade look mild. I don't want health outreach going to the wrong place because I picked the convenient dataset. What's the honest way to choose?

A pragmatic approach is to treat LST as a proxy and test how well it predicts air temperature in your city before relying on it. If you can find any street-level air temperature observations, even a few dozen points from a mobile traverse or fixed loggers, regress air temperature on LST plus land-cover variables like canopy fraction and building density. If the fit is weak or biased in particular land-cover types, you can either model air temperature directly or present LST with clear caveats. Many cities also combine an exposure layer with a population layer so that unoccupied hot surfaces are down-weighted in the final vulnerability index.

I help coordinate a group of neighbourhood volunteers who've put up about forty low-cost sensors on balconies and fences. They log temperature, humidity and fine particulate matter every few minutes. People are really enthusiastic, but when I look at the raw data some units read two or three degrees warmer than their neighbours for no obvious reason. Before I go further, what are the common reasons cheap sensors disagree like this?

Low-cost sensor disagreement usually comes from a few sources. Siting is the biggest one for temperature: a sensor in direct sun, against a south-facing wall, or without a radiation shield will read high during the day. Unit-to-unit manufacturing variation adds a fixed offset, often a degree or so. Self-heating from electronics in a closed enclosure can bias readings upward. For particulate sensors, humidity is a major issue, because optical counters see swollen water-coated particles and overestimate mass at high relative humidity. Finally, there is drift, where a sensor's response slowly changes over months as components age or get dirty.

Okay, siting is probably part of it, we gave people instructions but I doubt everyone followed them. Honestly though, even when I compare two units sitting side by side on my own balcony they diverge over a couple of months. So I think we have both fixed offsets and drift. Is there a simple fix, or is this a real statistics problem?

Side-by-side divergence over months points to genuine drift, and that is more than a one-off fix. A common first step is a co-location period: put all units next to a reference-grade instrument for a week or two, fit a per-unit correction, then deploy. But drift means that correction decays, so you need periodic re-co-location or a statistical method that tracks drift over time, for example using a reference station as an anchor and modelling each sensor's bias as a slowly varying function. It is a well-studied but genuinely nontrivial problem.

chats.title: How much do street trees cool?

messages.text: I'm trying to get a realistic number for how much street trees actually cool a neighbourhood. Advocacy materials throw around figures like ten degrees cooler, which I suspect is surface temperature under a single tree. What does the literature say about air temperature cooling at the block or neighbourhood scale as canopy cover increases?

You are right to be suspicious of the headline numbers. Shaded surfaces can be 10 to 20 degrees cooler than sunlit pavement, but air temperature effects are much smaller. Studies using dense air temperature measurements typically find daytime cooling on the order of 0.5 to 2 degrees between low-canopy and high-canopy blocks, with the effect often nonlinear: cooling accelerates once canopy cover passes roughly 40 percent, because shading becomes continuous and evapotranspiration adds up. Effects also depend on tree species, irrigation, street orientation, and wind, and night-time effects can be weak or even slightly reversed under dense canopy that traps longwave radiation.

The nonlinearity is interesting. In our city most of the lower-income blocks are around ten or fifteen percent canopy, so if the real benefits only kick in near forty percent, planting a few trees here and there might do very little for heat. I'd like to estimate what it would actually take to move those blocks into the range where cooling becomes meaningful.

That is a useful framing for planners. You could estimate the number of additional trees needed by working from crown area: divide the target canopy area increase by the expected mature crown area of suitable species, then adjust for mortality, since street trees in harsh sites often have high early loss. Be careful to note that mature canopy takes 15 to 25 years, so short-term heat relief may need complementary measures like cool pavements or shade structures. A scenario table with canopy targets, tree counts, and expected cooling ranges would make the trade-offs transparent.

Follow-up on our volunteer sensors. There's one regulatory air monitoring station about three kilometres from most of our units. I've been thinking about using it as a reference to correct our particulate readings, but I'm not sure that's legit since the sensors aren't at the same spot. My stats background is pretty basic, I can do a linear regression but not much beyond that. How would someone who knows this field approach it?

Using a distant reference is common, but it needs care. For fine particulate matter, regional background often dominates, so concentrations three kilometres apart can be strongly correlated on hourly or daily timescales, which supports using the station as a reference. Typical approaches include multiple linear regression with relative humidity and temperature as covariates, nonlinear humidity corrections based on particle hygroscopic growth, and machine-learning models like random forests trained during co-location. More advanced methods treat the network jointly, for example using a spatial statistical model where sensors share information and the reference station anchors the overall level.

Honestly the joint spatial model sounds like what we need, but I don't think I can build it myself and do it properly. I'd rather find someone with a real statistics or atmospheric measurement background who'd want to work with us. We have two years of data from forty sensors, which seems like a decent dataset for a methods person. Does that sound like something a researcher would find interesting?

Very likely, yes. Two years from forty neighbourhood sensors with a nearby reference station is a valuable dataset for methods development, especially for studying drift and humidity effects over seasons. Statisticians working on measurement error, spatio-temporal models, or data fusion, and atmospheric scientists working on low-cost sensor evaluation, would both find it interesting. It helps to prepare a short description: number of units, variables, sampling interval, gaps, known siting issues, and what decisions the corrected data will support. That makes it easy for a potential collaborator to judge the fit.

Another question on the satellite versus street-level problem. The thermal imagery I have comes from a mid-morning overpass, but the heat risk for people is mostly late afternoon and overnight. I have a handful of air temperature loggers from a city pilot, and they show the hottest blocks at 5pm aren't always the hottest blocks in the morning image. How much should I trust a morning snapshot for this?

Your loggers are showing a real effect. Surface heating in the morning is driven by sun angle and surface properties, so east-facing and dark surfaces heat first. By late afternoon, accumulated heat storage in buildings and pavements, plus reduced ventilation in dense street canyons, can shift the hotspots. At night the pattern can change again, with dense built-up areas retaining heat while open green areas cool quickly. A single morning image captures one phase of that cycle. If possible, check whether any afternoon or night-time thermal acquisitions exist, and use your loggers to quantify how well the morning pattern ranks blocks at the times that matter for health.

I checked and there's one night-time scene from last summer, but it's partly cloudy. When I compared the loggers to the morning LST, the rank correlation was only around 0.5, which is honestly worse than I expected. I'm starting to think the satellite layer is fine for showing where surfaces are hot but not good enough to decide where people are at risk.

A rank correlation of 0.5 suggests the morning image captures part of the pattern but misses a lot, so your conclusion is reasonable. One option is to use the night-time scene for the cloud-free areas only, since night-time surface and air temperatures tend to agree more closely than daytime ones. Another is to treat LST as one predictor among several rather than as the exposure layer itself. Either way, documenting that 0.5 figure in your methods is valuable, because it shows readers why you did not rely on the satellite data alone.

I'm still fighting with drift in our volunteer temperature sensors. Some units seem to slowly read warmer over the summer and then come back in autumn, which makes me think it's partly dust on the radiation shields and partly seasonal sun angle. I tried subtracting a monthly offset relative to the reference station but it feels hacky and I'm not confident I'm not just removing real local differences. How do people separate drift from genuine local signal?

That is the core identifiability challenge. If you correct every sensor to match the reference, you erase the real spatial differences you care about. Common strategies separate timescales: real local differences tend to show up as consistent diurnal patterns tied to land cover, while drift is slow and monotonic or seasonal. Methods include modelling each sensor's bias as a smooth function of time with a penalty, using periods of strong wind and well-mixed conditions as calibration windows when true spatial differences should be small, and rotating a travelling reference unit around the network. Hierarchical Bayesian models can formalise this by sharing information across sensors.

The well-mixed windy periods idea is clever, I hadn't thought of that. But I'm out of my depth with hierarchical Bayesian anything. This is really the bottleneck for us. The data are only useful if people trust them, and right now I can't defend the corrections. I need a collaborator who actually does measurement-error statistics.

That is a reasonable conclusion, and it is common for community monitoring projects to partner with a statistician at exactly this stage. You might frame the collaboration around a clear deliverable, such as a documented, reproducible correction pipeline with uncertainty estimates for each sensor-hour. That gives the methods person a publishable contribution and gives your volunteers data they can defend. Meanwhile, keep logging metadata like shield cleaning dates and any relocations, since those events are extremely valuable for separating drift from real signal.

I've been mapping where new street trees were planted over the last decade, and it's pretty clear they went disproportionately to neighbourhoods that already had decent canopy and higher incomes. Part of it seems to be that the planting program was request-based, so residents had to ask. I want to make the equity argument carefully rather than just showing a map that looks bad. How would you frame this analytically?

A careful framing would separate distribution of outcomes from the mechanism. First, quantify the disparity: plantings per kilometre of street or per available planting site, stratified by income or vulnerability quintile, with confidence intervals. Second, test the mechanism: if the program was request-based, compare request rates across neighbourhoods and the approval rate given a request. If requests drive the disparity, the policy lever is outreach or switching to proactive planting. Also account for physical constraints like sidewalk width and overhead wires, since critics will argue some neighbourhoods simply have fewer plantable sites.

Good point about plantable sites, the narrow sidewalks in the older dense areas are a real constraint. I also wonder whether tree survival differs, because planting a tree that dies in two years isn't really canopy. I'd like to estimate surviving canopy gain by neighbourhood rather than just counts of plantings. Is there usually data for that?

Sometimes. Many city forestry departments keep an inventory with planting date and status updates, and some record removals. If that is incomplete, you can estimate survival by comparing planting locations against later high-resolution imagery or lidar canopy maps to see whether a crown developed. Survival is often lower in low-income areas due to harsher sites, less watering, and more vandalism or construction damage, which would compound the equity gap. Presenting surviving canopy gain per resident by neighbourhood would be a strong, defensible metric.

I think I've convinced myself that for the vulnerability map I should be estimating air temperature, not using land-surface temperature directly. My plan is to train a model on the pilot loggers using LST, canopy fraction, building height and distance to water as predictors, then predict across the city. But I only have about thirty loggers. Is that enough, or am I going to overfit and produce a pretty map that's mostly noise?

Thirty loggers is limited but workable if you keep the model simple and validate honestly. With few stations, a regularised linear model or a generalised additive model with a handful of predictors is safer than a flexible machine-learning model. Use spatial cross-validation, leaving out clusters of nearby loggers, because random cross-validation overstates skill when stations are close together. Also check whether your loggers cover the full range of conditions in the city; if none sit in industrial zones, predictions there are extrapolations. Reporting a prediction uncertainty map alongside the estimate is good practice.

Yeah, coverage is a problem, none of the pilot loggers are in the industrial east side or the newest suburbs. So the model would basically be guessing there. I suppose I could flag those areas as low confidence. I still find it frustrating that the satellite data covers everything but measures the wrong thing, and the ground data measures the right thing but covers almost nothing.

That tension is exactly why fusion approaches exist: the satellite provides spatial coverage and pattern, and ground data provide the anchor for what people experience. Flagging low-confidence areas is honest and useful. If you can add even a few temporary loggers in the unsampled land-cover types during the next hot season, the gain in confidence would likely be disproportionate, because you would be filling the gaps the model cannot extrapolate across.

Our volunteers want to publish the sensor data openly on a public dashboard, which I support, but I'm nervous about putting up numbers that I know are biased. If a unit is reading three degrees high because of drift and a local journalist picks it up, that undermines the whole project. Should we hold off until the calibration problem is solved, or publish raw with warnings?

Many community networks handle this with data quality tiers. Publish raw data for transparency, but clearly separate it from a corrected or quality-controlled product, and display quality flags for each sensor, such as drift suspected, siting non-standard, or recently co-located. Dashboards can default to showing only data that passed basic checks. Including versioned correction methods in documentation also helps, so when you improve the calibration later, you can reprocess historical data and explain the change.

Tiers make sense. The awkward part is that our corrected tier doesn't really exist yet, because I still don't have a calibration method I'd stand behind. We need someone with stronger stats who can help design the correction properly. Until then I might just publish raw with flags and a big note that a calibrated version is coming.

That is a sensible interim plan. A visible roadmap note can actually help recruit help, since it signals to potential collaborators that there is a concrete, well-defined methods problem with real users waiting. When you approach someone, offer co-authorship on a methods paper and a clear scope, for example a correction pipeline for temperature and fine particulate matter using the reference station and co-location periods, so they can see the size of the commitment.

I'm drafting a short memo for the city's urban forestry team arguing that canopy targets should be set per neighbourhood instead of a single citywide percentage. A citywide target of thirty percent can be met while the hottest, lowest-income areas stay at ten. I want to tie the argument to the cooling evidence and the planting history. Can you help me structure it?

A clear structure could be: first, the problem, showing that the current citywide average masks a wide range across neighbourhoods; second, why it matters, summarising evidence that cooling benefits are nonlinear and concentrated above certain canopy thresholds, so averages are misleading; third, the historical pattern, showing that past plantings went disproportionately to already-green areas and that survival may be lower in harsher sites; fourth, the proposal, neighbourhood-level minimum canopy targets prioritised by heat exposure and vulnerability; and finally implementation, including proactive planting, maintenance funding for early establishment, and monitoring surviving canopy rather than planting counts.

That's close to what I had in mind. I'm unsure how strongly to state the cooling numbers, since the honest range is maybe one or two degrees of air temperature, which sounds small to a non-expert. I don't want to oversell it, but I also think even one degree matters for heat-related illness on the worst days.

You can present the modest number honestly and then translate it. Explain that one to two degrees of air temperature is the average effect, while shaded pedestrians experience much larger reductions in radiant heat, which strongly affects thermal comfort. You can also note that health risk rises steeply on the hottest days, so small temperature reductions during extreme events can matter disproportionately. Being upfront about the uncertainty will make the memo more credible to technical readers.
